stories.title: Support for the Brothers
stories.keyVerse: "Beloved, follow not that which is evil, but that which is good. He that doeth good is of God: but he that doeth evil hath not seen God."
stories.text:
The elder unto the wellbeloved Gaius, whom I love in the truth.
Beloved, I wish above all things that thou mayest prosper and be in health, even as thy soul prospereth.
For I rejoiced greatly, when the brethren came and testified of the truth that is in thee, even as thou walkest in the truth.
I have no greater joy than to hear that my children walk in truth.
Beloved, thou doest faithfully whatsoever thou doest to the brethren, and to strangers;
Which have borne witness of thy charity before the church: whom if thou bring forward on their journey after a godly sort, thou shalt do well:
Because that for his name’s sake they went forth, taking nothing of the Gentiles.
We therefore ought to receive such, that we might be fellowhelpers to the truth.
I wrote unto the church: but Diotrephes, who loveth to have the preeminence among them, receiveth us not.
Wherefore, if I come, I will remember his deeds which he doeth, prating against us with malicious words: and not content therewith, neither doth he himself receive the brethren, and forbiddeth them that would, and casteth
them out of the church.
Beloved, follow not that which is evil, but that which is good. He that doeth good is of God: but he that doeth evil hath not seen God.
Demetrius hath good report of all
men, and of the truth itself: yea, and we
also bear record; and ye know that our record is true.
I had many things to write, but I will not with ink and pen write unto thee:
But I trust I shall shortly see thee, and we shall speak face to face. Peace
be to thee.
Our friends salute thee. Greet the friends by name.
stories.retelling:
The elder's letter to Gaius began with warmth and sincerity, his words a tangible embrace spanning the distance between them. As he sat at his desk, he envisioned Gaius—steadfast and true—his spirit as vibrant as the sunlit fields outside his window. He wished for Gaius not only prosperity and health but for his soul to flourish in truth.

His heart swelled with joy recalling the reports from the traveling brothers, who spoke of Gaius's unwavering integrity and kindness. Gaius had a reputation for his devotion, extending hospitality not just to familiar faces but to strangers as well. The brothers had come back praising Gaius's generosity, which had become the talk of the assembly. The elder, feeling a surge of paternal pride, knew no greater happiness than seeing his spiritual children embody the truth.

He urged Gaius to continue supporting these travelers, emphasizing that by aiding them, he was contributing to a higher cause. These men journeyed in the name of faith, relying not on the resources of the Gentiles, but on the support of their fellow believers. The elder emphasized the importance of welcoming such workers, to be partners in spreading the truth.

However, not all was well. The elder's tone shifted as he recounted troubles with Diotrephes, a man who craved authority and recognition, rejecting the elder's guidance. Diotrephes slandered them with malicious words, refusing to welcome the brothers and expelling those who wished to help. The elder's resolve hardened. **"Beloved, follow not that which is evil, but that which is good,"** he cautioned Gaius, urging him to choose the path of righteousness. Diotrephes's actions were a stark reminder of the harm that comes from seeking power over truth.

In contrast, the elder mentioned Demetrius, a man of good repute, known for his honesty and alignment with the truth. Here was an example to emulate, a beacon of integrity amidst the chaos. The elder assured Gaius of Demetrius's commendable character, aligning his testimony with the collective witness of the community.

As the letter drew to a close, the elder expressed reluctance to fill the page with more words. Instead, he longed for the warmth of personal conversation. He hoped soon to meet Gaius face to face, where words could flow freely without the constraints of ink and parchment. Until that time, he extended peace to Gaius, a gentle benediction to sustain him.

The elder concluded with a heartfelt greeting from mutual friends, encouraging Gaius to pass along these warm regards individually. Each name, spoken with affection, bridged the distance between them, reinforcing the bonds of their shared faith.
